phy-r-008.background: Charge comes in two kinds, and the rule for how they behave is the first thing to fix in your head because everything else leans on it: LIKE charges repel, UNLIKE charges attract. Gravity has no equivalent, since mass only ever attracts, which is why electric forces can hold matter together at all. An atom exists because the negative electrons are pulled towards the positive nucleus while pushing each other apart.
phy-r-008.find: Whether two electrons placed near each other attract or repel
steps: Identify the sign of each: an electron is NEGATIVE.
Both are negative, so the two charges are LIKE.
Like charges repel, so the statement is FALSE. They repel.
Coulomb's law agrees: the product of two negatives is positive, and a positive force in the convention means repulsion.
phy-r-008.check: Ask what would happen if it were otherwise. If electrons attracted each other, every electron cloud in every atom would collapse in on itself and matter would not have volume. The fact that you cannot push your hand through a table is the repulsion between electrons, felt at everyday scale.

phy-r-012.background: Coulomb's law is an INVERSE SQUARE law, and the square is the part that catches people. Move a charge further away and the force does not fall in proportion to the distance; it falls in proportion to the distance squared. The reason is geometric: the influence spreads out over the surface of a sphere, and a sphere's area grows as r², so the same influence is spread over more area and thinned by that same factor.
phy-r-012.find: The word that completes: tripling the distance drops the force to one ___
phy-r-012.why: The whole question lives in the r² on the bottom. Because the distance is squared, tripling it multiplies the bottom by 3² = 9, so the force is divided by 9, not by 3.
symbols: F = the force, in newtons
r = the separation, and it is SQUARED
k = the Coulomb constant, unchanged by the move
steps: The answer is NINTH.
Original force:  F ∝ 1 ÷ r²
Triple the distance:  the new bottom is (3r)² = 9r²
So the new force is F ÷ 9, one ninth of the original.
Why not third: that is what would happen if the law were 1 ÷ r rather than 1 ÷ r².
Why not sixth or twelfth: neither 6 nor 12 is a square, and an inverse square law can only ever divide by a square number.
phy-r-012.check: Test the same move on POTENTIAL, which has a plain r rather than r². Tripling the distance would drop the potential to one third, not one ninth. That contrast is worth holding, because examiners set the two questions side by side to see whether you noticed which quantity has the square.

phy-r-033.background: Put a charge inside a hollow metal box and the free electrons in the metal shuffle around until the field they create exactly cancels the field inside the metal itself. That is why a car or an aeroplane protects you from lightning, and it is called a Faraday cage. But the cancellation applies to the region with NO enclosed charge; put a charge in the hollow and there is certainly a field in there.
phy-r-033.find: Whether the statement is true, and what the qualification is doing
phy-r-033.why: Gauss's law is what proves it. Draw an imaginary closed surface inside the cavity. If it encloses no charge then the total flux through it is zero, and by symmetry that forces the field itself to be zero everywhere on it. The moment a charge is enclosed, the right-hand side is no longer zero and neither is the field.
symbols: Φ = the total flux through the imaginary closed surface
Q = the charge ENCLOSED by that surface, which is the whole point
ε₀ = the permittivity of free space
steps: The statement is TRUE, and the qualification is load-bearing.
Draw an imaginary closed surface inside the cavity.
No charge is enclosed, so Q = 0 and the flux is zero.
By the symmetry of the situation, zero flux everywhere means zero field.
Remove the qualification and it breaks: enclose a charge and there is a field.
phy-r-033.check: Sort out which zero you are talking about, since three different regions get confused. Inside the metal itself the field is always zero in electrostatics, whatever is around. Inside an EMPTY cavity the field is zero. Inside a cavity CONTAINING a charge the field is not zero. The word enclosed is what separates the three cases.

phy-r-041.background: Capacitance is charge per volt, and the striking thing is that this ratio is FIXED for a given capacitor. Put more charge on and the voltage rises in exact proportion, so the ratio does not budge. That means capacitance cannot depend on how much charge or voltage you happen to be using; it depends only on how the thing is built, which means its shape, its size, and what is between the plates.
phy-r-041.find: The word that completes: capacitance is fixed by the capacitor's ___
phy-r-041.formula: C = ε₀ εr A over d
phy-r-041.why: Every quantity on the right-hand side is a fact about the construction: the plate area, the gap, and the material filling it. Neither Q nor V appears anywhere, which is the algebraic statement of the answer.
symbols: A = the plate area, part of the geometry
d = the plate separation, part of the geometry
εr = the dielectric constant of the filling, a property of the material
ε₀ = a constant of nature, not of this capacitor
steps: The answer is GEOMETRY.
Why not charge: doubling the charge doubles the voltage too, so C = Q ÷ V is unchanged.
Why not voltage: the same argument the other way round.
Why not temperature: real dielectrics do drift a little with temperature, but that is a second-order imperfection, not what sets the value.
phy-r-041.check: Look at the parallel plate formula and ask which symbols could change without rebuilding the capacitor. A and d cannot, εr cannot, ε₀ certainly cannot. Nothing in it can vary with use, which is precisely why capacitance is quoted as a fixed number on the component itself.

phy-r-045.background: Resistors and capacitors combine by opposite rules, and knowing WHY stops you having to memorise two of everything. Put resistors in series and the current must fight through both, so resistance adds. Put capacitors in parallel and you have effectively built one capacitor with more plate area, so capacitance adds. Series capacitors behave like one capacitor with a wider gap, which makes them worse, hence the reciprocals.
phy-r-045.find: The word that completes: capacitors add when they are in ___
steps: The answer is PARALLEL.
Parallel capacitors share the same two terminals, so it is as if the plates were made bigger, and bigger area means more capacitance: C = C₁ + C₂.
Series capacitors sit one behind the other, like a single capacitor with a wider gap, so the total is SMALLER than either: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
Resistors do the reverse, adding in series.
Why not opposition or phase: those belong to a.c. circuits and reactance, not to combining capacitance.
phy-r-045.check: One sentence carries both rules: capacitors are backwards from resistors. So work out the resistor case, which most people find natural, and then flip it. And you always have an independent guard on the answer, since a series combination must come out SMALLER than the smallest item in it, while a parallel one must come out larger than the largest.

phy-r-052.background: Resistance is not a property of a material alone; it is a property of a particular PIECE of it. Resistivity ρ is the material's own contribution, the same for any piece of copper. Turn that into the resistance of an actual wire and two pieces of geometry enter: how far the current must travel, and how wide a road it has to travel on. A long thin wire is a long narrow road, and traffic crawls.
phy-r-052.find: The word that completes: long and ___ resists, while short and fat does not
phy-r-052.why: The formula is the sentence. L is on top, so more length means more resistance. A is underneath, so more area means less resistance. Long and thin puts both factors in the unfavourable direction at once, which is why it resists most.
symbols: R = the resistance of this particular piece, in ohms
ρ = the resistivity, a property of the MATERIAL, in Ω m
L = the length of the wire, in metres, on TOP
A = the cross-sectional area, in m², UNDERNEATH
steps: The answer is THIN.
Length on top:  longer means more resistance.
Area underneath:  thinner means less area, so more resistance.
Long and thin therefore resists the most, short and fat the least.
Why not cold: cooling a metal actually LOWERS its resistance, which is the opposite direction.
Why not straight: bending a wire does not change its length or its cross-section, so it changes nothing.
phy-r-052.check: Guard the area, because that is where the marks actually go. For a round wire A = πr², so halving the radius does not halve the area, it quarters it, and therefore QUADRUPLES the resistance. Any question that gives you a radius or a diameter rather than an area is testing exactly that step.

phy-r-056.background: Kirchhoff's two laws look like circuit rules but they are conservation laws in disguise, which is why they are always true and never approximations. Charge cannot be created or destroyed, so it cannot pile up at a junction: whatever flows in must flow out. Energy cannot be created either, so a charge carried all the way round a loop and back to where it started must have gained exactly as much as it lost.
phy-r-056.find: The word that completes: the current law is about charge and the voltage law is about ___
steps: The answer is ENERGY.
The current law, at a junction:  ΣI in = ΣI out, which is conservation of CHARGE.
The voltage law, round a loop:  Σ emf = Σ IR, which is conservation of ENERGY.
Why not charge: that is already the current law, and the pair would then say the same thing twice.
Why not power or resistance: neither is a conserved quantity, and conservation is the whole basis of both laws.
phy-r-056.check: Hold it as one sentence: junctions conserve charge, loops conserve energy. Then use the shape of the circuit to pick the law. A junction, meaning a place where wires meet, calls for the current law. A closed loop you can trace with a finger calls for the voltage law. Most problems need one of each.

phy-r-071.background: The electron and the proton carry the same size of charge but wildly different masses, and that single asymmetry runs through the whole of this course. It is why the electron does almost all the moving in a current, why it curves far more tightly in a magnetic field, and why the nucleus can be treated as sitting still while electrons orbit it.
phy-r-071.find: The exponent in the electron mass, 9.11 × 10 to the power minus ___
steps: The answer is 31.
Compare the two:  10⁻²⁷ ÷ 10⁻³¹ = 10⁴, so the proton is about 10000 times heavier by the powers alone.
Include the front numbers:  1.67 ÷ 9.11 is about 0.18, so the true ratio is about 1836.
Why not 27: that is the PROTON, and the two are deliberately offered together.
Why not 19: that is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹, the elementary CHARGE, not a mass.
Why not 12: that is 8.85 × 10⁻¹², the permittivity ε₀.
phy-r-071.check: Sort the four constants by what they measure rather than by their digits, since the digits are what the options play on. 10⁻³¹ and 10⁻²⁷ are masses in kilograms, 10⁻¹⁹ is a charge in coulombs, and 10⁻¹² is ε₀ in farads per metre. Ask what UNIT the answer needs and only one candidate survives.

phy-r-073.background: The proton is the heavy partner. About 1836 times the mass of an electron, which is why in a wire it is the electrons that drift while the positive ions stay put, vibrating in the lattice. In a magnetic field the same mass difference means a proton curves on a far wider arc than an electron at the same speed, since r = mv ÷ qB puts mass on the top.
given: Electron mass, for contrast:  mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg
phy-r-073.find: The exponent in the proton mass, 1.67 × 10 to the power minus ___
steps: The answer is 27.
A less negative exponent means a BIGGER number, and the proton is the heavier one.
So the proton's −27 must sit above the electron's −31, which it does.
Why not 31: that is the electron, the light one.
Why not 19 or 12: those are the elementary charge and ε₀, neither of which is a mass.
phy-r-073.check: Use the sign as the check rather than memory alone. Between 10⁻²⁷ and 10⁻³¹, the one closer to zero is larger, so it must belong to the heavier particle. If you ever attach −31 to the proton, the mass ratio comes out upside down and a proton becomes lighter than an electron, which contradicts everything the course says about which particle moves.

phy-r-075.background: A magnetic field only acts on the part of a charge's motion that CUTS ACROSS the field lines. Move exactly along them and you cut nothing, so you feel nothing. This is the deep difference between the magnetic force and the electric force: an electric field pushes a charge whether it moves or not, and always along the field, while a magnetic field pushes only moving charges and always at right angles to their motion.
phy-r-075.find: The value of sin 0 that makes the force vanish
phy-r-075.why: The angle θ is measured between the VELOCITY and the FIELD. Moving along the field makes that angle zero, and sin 0 = 0, so the whole force collapses to nothing however fast the charge is going and however strong the field is.
symbols: F = the magnetic force, in newtons
q = the charge, in coulombs
v = the speed, in m s⁻¹
B = the flux density, in teslas
θ = the angle between v and B, taking SINE
steps: The answer is 0.
Moving ALONG the field means θ = 0°.
F = qvB × 0 = 0, so there is no force at all.
Why not 1: that is sin 90°, motion straight across the field, which gives the MAXIMUM force.
Why not 0.5: that is sin 30°, and why not 90: that is an angle, not a sine.
phy-r-075.check: Keep the two trigonometric functions apart by their zero cases. FORCE uses sine, so it is zero when the motion is along the field. FLUX uses cosine, so it is zero when the surface is edge-on to the field. Ask yourself which quantity is being asked for and the function follows, which stops the single commonest error in this whole module.

phy-r-079.background: A charged particle circling in a magnetic field completes each lap in the same time no matter how fast it is going. Speed it up and it swings out onto a wider circle, but the extra distance exactly cancels the extra speed, so the time per lap does not change. That surprising fact is what makes the cyclotron possible: a fixed alternating voltage at one fixed frequency can keep accelerating the particle lap after lap.
phy-r-079.find: The quantity the cyclotron frequency does NOT depend on
phy-r-079.why: Read the formula and notice what is absent. Charge, field and mass all appear; speed and radius do not. That is the whole answer, and it is more reliable than trying to remember a sentence about it.
symbols: f = the cyclotron frequency, in hertz, the laps per second
q = the charge on the particle, in coulombs
B = the flux density, in teslas
m = the mass of the particle, in kilograms
2π = the pure number that turns radians per second into laps per second
steps: The answer is SPEED.
Start from the radius:  r = mv ÷ (qB), so a faster particle takes a wider circle.
One lap is a distance 2πr, covered at speed v, so the time is T = 2πr ÷ v.
Substitute r:  T = 2π(mv ÷ qB) ÷ v, and the v cancels top and bottom.
T = 2πm ÷ (qB), and f = 1 ÷ T = qB ÷ (2πm), with no v anywhere.
Why not charge, mass or field: all three are visibly present in the formula.
phy-r-079.check: The cancellation is the proof, and it is worth writing out rather than accepting: the v that arrives with the wider radius is the same v that carries the particle round faster, so the two cancel exactly. This is also why a cyclotron eventually fails at very high energies, since relativity makes the mass grow and the frequency then does drift.

phy-r-081.background: μ₀ is written as 4π × 10⁻⁷ rather than as 1.257 × 10⁻⁶, and the odd form is deliberate. Almost every magnetic formula for a wire or a toroid carries a 2π or a 4π underneath, so keeping the π visible on top lets it cancel by eye instead of by calculator. That single habit removes the commonest arithmetic error in the whole module.
given: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹, the permeability of free space
phy-r-081.find: The exponent in 4π × 10 to the power minus ___
phy-r-081.why: Substituting μ₀ into the straight wire law shows why the form is chosen. The 4π on top and the 2π underneath cancel down to 2, leaving B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × I ÷ r, which needs no π at all.
symbols: μ₀ = the permeability of free space, in henries per metre
I = the current, in amperes
r = the distance from the wire, in metres
2 × 10⁻⁷ = what μ₀ ÷ 2π simplifies to exactly
steps: The answer is 7.
μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹.
In the wire formula:  4π ÷ 2π = 2, so B = (2 × 10⁻⁷ × I) ÷ r.
Why not 12: that is 8.85 × 10⁻¹², which is ε₀, the ELECTRIC partner.
Why not 19: that is the elementary charge, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Why not 9: that is 9 × 10⁹, the Coulomb constant, and it is POSITIVE.
phy-r-081.check: Pair the two constants of free space so neither can be reached for by mistake: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² is electric, μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ is magnetic. Their product is 1 ÷ c², which is the relation Maxwell used to identify light. If you can state that link you will never confuse the two.

phy-r-091.background: Faraday's law is about CHANGE, and that is genuinely counter-intuitive. A coil sitting in the strongest magnetic field ever built produces no voltage at all, provided nothing is moving. Push a magnet towards a coil and a voltage appears; stop with the magnet inside and it disappears; pull it out and it appears again with the opposite sign. What the coil responds to is not the flux but the rate at which the flux changes.
phy-r-091.find: The key word in Faraday's law
phy-r-091.why: The Δ symbols are the answer written in algebra. It is ΔΦ, the CHANGE in flux, divided by Δt, the time it took. Both are differences; neither is an amount. A steady flux gives ΔΦ = 0 and therefore no emf.
symbols: emf = the induced voltage, in volts
N = the number of turns, which multiplies the result
ΔΦ = the CHANGE in flux, in webers
Δt = the time over which it changed, in seconds
the minus sign = Lenz's law, the induced effect opposing the change
steps: The answer is CHANGE.
A steady flux, however large, gives ΔΦ = 0 and therefore no emf.
Why not strength: a strong but constant field induces nothing whatsoever.
Why not area: changing the area is one WAY to change the flux, but it is not the key idea, and rotating the loop works just as well.
Why not direction: the same objection, since it is one route to a change rather than the principle.
phy-r-091.check: Test yourself with the generator, which settles it. A generator spins a coil between magnets of FIXED strength and produces a steady supply of electricity. Nothing about the field is changing, only the angle of the coil, so the flux BA cos θ changes because of the cosine. Only the word change survives that test; strength, area and direction all fail it.
